screens.title: What is an Error Handling Boundary?
screens.narratorSegment: An error handling boundary is a deliberate place in your architecture where exceptions stop propagating and are either handled, logged, or translated to a different type. This is not an ad-hoc catch anywhere — it is a boundary chosen because that layer has the right context to make a sensible decision. For example, the data access layer knows about S Q L errors and constraints and can translate a unique-constraint violation into a DuplicateEntryError. The business logic layer knows user creation rules and can translate that into UserAlreadyExistsException. The presentation layer knows how to render messages for users and should not be forced to examine S Q L state codes. An important misconception to avoid is thinking every exception must be handled as soon as it appears. Catching too early robs higher layers of context and often leads to leaking technical details into user-facing logic. Another common mistake is catching too broadly; blanket catches hide failures like configuration errors or memory issues. A practical heuristic is: catch where you can do one of three things with confidence — recover, enrich/translate, or fail with context. Example: when a file write fails in a storage module, that module logs the stack trace and raises DataStorageError; callers then show a friendly message. Takeaway: choose boundaries that have the data and intent to act correctly, and avoid catching exceptions without a clear handling strategy. Where in your codebase are you currently catching broad exceptions? Could that be moved to a more contextual boundary?

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › What is an Error Handling Boundary?
Boundary definition
A chosen layer point that can meaningfully handle, log, or translate an exception.
Why boundaries matter
  • Keep layers focused on their concerns and avoid leaking technical details.
  • Allow translation to domain errors where business context exists.
  • Place structured logging where it will capture meaningful context.
Misconception
Catching everything early hides context and can mask critical failures.
Concrete example
A DAL sees a SQL unique constraint violation. It logs the SQL error and raises DuplicateEntryError. The BLL translates that into UserAlreadyExistsException. The PL shows a friendly message to the user.
Takeaway
Catch where you can recover or add context; translate when you can make the error meaningful to callers.
Check your code
Search for broad catches and ask: can this be moved to a boundary with more context?

screens.title: Error Flow in a 3‑Tier Application
screens.narratorSegment: A three-tier application—Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access—creates natural boundaries for error handling. Errors originate in low-level components like the database, filesystem, or network. The Data Access Layer is responsible for catching technical exceptions such as S Q L errors or IO failures, logging technical details, and then re-throwing a more abstract exception like DatabaseAccessException. The Business Logic Layer receives that higher-level error and, depending on context, may translate it further into a business exception such as UserAlreadyExistsException or PaymentProcessingFailedException. Finally, the Presentation Layer maps business exceptions to user-friendly messages and HTTP responses. A concrete example: a unique constraint violation in the database becomes DuplicateEntryError in the DAL, then UserAlreadyExistsException in the BLL, and finally a 409 conflict with a friendly message in the UI. A common mistake is to let the presentation layer catch raw S Q L exceptions and generate messages using low-level details; that exposes internals and confuses users. Another subtle point: logging must occur at boundaries where the log entry can include meaningful contextual fields. If you log only in low-level code without business context, operational teams may struggle to understand the impact. Where in your stack can you attach identifiers like request ID, user ID, or operation name so logs are actionable?

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Error Flow in a 3‑Tier Application
3-Tier flow
Data Access Layer (DAL)
Catches SQL/IO errors, logs technical details, and raises abstract DAL exceptions.
Business Logic Layer (BLL)
Translates DAL exceptions to business exceptions and decides recovery or escalation.
Presentation Layer (PL)
Converts business exceptions into user-facing messages or status codes.
Concrete scenario
A database unique constraint fails during user creation. The DAL logs SQL details and raises DuplicateEntryError. The BLL maps that to UserAlreadyExistsException. The PL returns a clear message: "A user with that email already exists."
Pro tip
Attach request and user identifiers to log entries at the boundary so operators can correlate events across services.
Common mistake
Catching raw SQL errors in the presentation layer and showing stack traces to users.

screens.title: Catch at the Appropriate Level
screens.narratorSegment: The phrase "catch at the appropriate level" means you should only catch exceptions in the layer that has enough information to do something useful: fix it, add context, or create a meaningful domain-level error. The practical effect is that each layer stays focused. For example, a DAL knows S Q L error codes and can recognize a unique constraint violation and transform it into a DuplicateEntryError. The BLL knows business rules and can convert that into UserAlreadyExistsException or use a compensating action. If you catch an error too early, say in a helper function deep inside the DAL, you remove knowledge that upstream logic might need to decide how to continue. Conversely, catching too broadly at high levels with a generic exception handler often hides programming errors and control flow bugs. A common misconception is believing that more catches equals more robustness — in fact, poorly placed catches reduce observability and can convert recoverable errors into silent failures. To decide where to catch, ask: can this layer produce a meaningful, context-enriched response to the caller? If yes, catch and handle there; if not, let it bubble to a boundary that can.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Catch at the Appropriate Level
Decision checklist
  • Can this layer recover? If yes, handle and log.
  • Can this layer translate into a meaningful domain error? If yes, translate and re-throw.
  • Otherwise, let it bubble to a boundary that can.
Example
DAL detects SQL unique-constraint → log details and raise DuplicateEntryError for BLL to interpret.
Contrast
Catching Exception globally or returning null obscures real failures and increases debugging time.
Pro tip
Prefer explicit exception types and avoid generic catches. This preserves observability and aids monitoring.
Common mistake
Using a generic catch-all to return a default value; this often hides failing invariants.

screens.title: Structured Logging Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Structured logging means emitting entries that are machine-readable, usually key-value pairs or JSON objects, rather than free-form text. This makes logs searchable, filterable, and easier to parse by aggregation tools. Essential fields to include are timestamp, level, message, logger name, module, function, line number, and contextual extras such as request ID, user ID, and operation name. When an exception occurs, include the stack trace so engineers can reconstruct the failure. A misconception is treating logs as informal notes — instead, treat them as structured telemetry that your monitoring and incident tooling will consume. For example, logging an error from a failed data save should include the filename, user identifier, and the original exception detail in an "exception" field. Structured logs also support different levels: DEBUG for verbose diagnostics, INFO for normal operation confirmations, WARNING for notable but non-fatal events, ERROR for failed functions, and CRITICAL for program-halting failures. Takeaway: pick a consistent schema, attach context at boundaries, and avoid mixing unstructured messages with important diagnosis fields. Structured Logging Fundamentals means emit machine-readable logs with consistent fields and contextual identifiers so incidents are traceable and searchable.. In practical terms, why structured logs are essential and what fields to include. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Structured Logging Fundamentals
Key fields for structured logs
  • timestamp, level, message
  • logger_name, module, func_name, line_no
  • context extras: request_id, user_id, operation, resource identifiers
  • exception: stack trace or serialized error info
Why structured logs help
They let teams filter by fields, correlate events across services, and automate alerting on important signals.
Example entry
{
  "timestamp": "2023-01-01T12:00:00Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "message": "Failed to save file",
  "logger_name": "DataService",
  "file": "storage.py",
  "exception": "Traceback (most recent call last): ...",
  "request_id": "req-12345",
  "user_id": 42
}
Takeaway
Design a small, consistent schema and emit logs with contextual extras at boundaries for tracing failures.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the provided Python example that implements a JsonFormatter for structured logging. The formatter builds a dictionary that includes timestamp, level, message, logger name, module, function name, and line number. If exc_info is present, it serializes the exception stack trace into an "exception" field. The code then dumps the dictionary as JSON, which makes each log entry machine-readable. A concrete use: a function that validates input raises ValueError; the logger writes an ERROR entry with exc_info=True and extra fields like data_id or input_data. A common misconception is that structured logging is only for large teams; in reality, even small services gain from predictable logs. Notice how the example configures a logger, attaches a StreamHandler, and sets level to DEBUG to capture development diagnostics. When moving to production, handlers may send entries to aggregation services rather than standard output. When reusing this pattern, ensure sensitive data is not emitted and that exception serialization is safe. content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › JsonFormatter Walkthrough
Key parts of the formatter
  • Collect timestamp, level, message, module, function, and line.
  • Attach exception text when exc_info is set.
  • Serialize dictionary with json.dumps for machine parsing.
Usage pattern
Create a logger, add a StreamHandler with JsonFormatter, set level, and call logger.info/error with extra fields for context.
Code excerpt
class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, record):
        log_entry = {
            "timestamp": self.formatTime(record, self.datefmt),
            "level": record.levelname,
            "message": record.getMessage(),
            "logger_name": record.name,
            "module": record.module,
            "func_name": record.funcName,
            "line_no": record.lineno,
        }
        if record.exc_info:
            log_entry["exception"] = self.formatException(record.exc_info)
        return json.dumps(log_entry)
Takeaway
Structured formatter centralizes log shaping so all handlers emit consistent, parsable entries.

screens.title: Log Levels: When to Use Each
screens.narratorSegment: Log levels enable you to categorize events by importance. DEBUG is for detailed developer-level traces that aid diagnosis but are usually too verbose for production. INFO confirms that operations completed as expected, like a job finishing or a user successfully signing in. WARNING flags unexpected but non-fatal situations that might indicate future problems, such as low disk space. ERROR indicates that a specific function failed to complete, for example, a failure to persist data for a particular request. CRITICAL signals a program-level failure that might require immediate attention. A practical example: when saving user data, use INFO for a successful save, ERROR if the database write fails for a single user, and CRITICAL if the database connection pool is exhausted and the whole service is degraded. A common mistake is logging everything at ERROR; that creates noise and masks real incidents. Another misconception is underusing DEBUG in development; rich debug entries during development shorten time-to-fix without flooding production systems if configured correctly. Takeaway: adopt consistent level usage and document it in your team so logs mean the same thing to everyone.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › save_data_to_file Pattern
Starter code (excerpt)
# Define custom exception
class DataStorageError(Exception):
    """Raised when there's a problem storing data."""
    pass

# save_data_to_file
try:
    with open(filename, 'w') as f:
        f.write(data)
    app_logger.info(f"Data successfully saved to {filename}")
except IOError as e:
    app_logger.error(f"Failed to write to file {filename}: {e}", exc_info=True)
    raise DataStorageError(f"Could not store data to '{filename}'. Please check path and permissions.")
Notes
The logger records technical details, exc_info=True adds the stack trace, and the custom exception hides low-level specifics from callers.
Concrete test steps
  1. Call save_data_to_file("output.txt", "Hello") – expect INFO and no exception.
  2. Call save_data_to_file("non_existent_dir/error.txt", "...") – expect ERROR with stack trace and DataStorageError for caller.
Takeaway
Translate and re-throw domain errors after logging technical detail so callers and users only see appropriate information.

screens.title: Where to Place Logging Statements
screens.narratorSegment: Logging is most useful when it is placed where context is available and it can be correlated with an operation. Place technical detail logs in lower layers but augment them at boundaries with contextual information such as request ID, user ID, and operation name. For example, a DAL might log the S Q L error and stack trace, while the service boundary logs the same event enriched with request and user identifiers so operators can trace the impact. Another important pattern is logging at the moment of handling or translation; when you translate a low-level exception to a domain error, log the translation step with both the original and the new error type. Avoid scattering logging calls deep in utility functions without context — those messages become hard to tie back to a single request. A common misconception is that more logs always equal better observability. Excessive DEBUG-level logs in production can obscure important events. Instead, sample or route verbose logs to separate collectors, and ensure ERROR and CRITICAL logs remain prominent. Takeaway: log at boundaries with correlated identifiers and make sure translation moments are clearly recorded.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Defensive Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring errors teams make when implementing error handling and logging. First, catching Exception everywhere hides programming errors and interrupts observability. Second, logging sensitive or low-level internal details to user-facing channels can expose secrets or confuse end users. Third, inconsistent log schemas across modules make aggregation and search painful. Defensive practices include: prefer specific exception types in catches; always include exc_info when logging exceptions so stack traces are captured; avoid emitting secrets in logs; and implement a single logging schema or formatter centrally so every service writes consistent fields. A concrete defensive example: wrap file system writes in a storage module that logs the stack trace and raises DataStorageError; centralize the JsonFormatter so all logs include the same keys; and ensure the presentation layer never logs raw exception traces for user operations. A practical check: run a failure scenario, then search your logs for request_id and confirm you find a trace across layers. This quick test catches schema drift and missing context early. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarise the core ideas to keep in mind. First, an error handling boundary is an intentional place to catch, translate, or log errors — choose boundaries that have the right context. Second, catch exceptions at the appropriate level: handle them where you can recover or translate, and avoid generic, early catches that hide failures. Third, implement structured logging with consistent fields and include exception details using exc_info so operators can reconstruct incidents. Fourth, use log levels intentionally: DEBUG for diagnostics, INFO for normal events, WARNING for concerning signs, ERROR for failed operations, and CRITICAL for system-level failures. These practices together improve observability, make incident response faster, and keep code clean and maintainable. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn to place error handling where it belongs, translate technical failures into meaningful domain errors, and record events with structured logs that aid debugging and monitoring. We will use the familiar three-layer architecture — presentation, business logic, and data access — to show how a low-level database failure becomes a user-friendly message after the right translations and logging. You will see practical patterns: catching exceptions at a boundary that has context, avoiding broad catches that hide issues, and using structured JSON-style logging with exception information and custom key-value fields. As you work through the examples and hands-on activity, you will practice writing a small file-saving service that logs errors with stack traces and raises a domain-specific storage error for callers to handle. By the end, you should be able to identify effective error boundaries in your own codebase, pick appropriate log levels for events, and implement exception translation that prevents technical details from leaking to users. Think about a recent bug you hunted — did logs help, or were they noisy and unstructured? We'll fix that.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to identify appropriate error handling boundaries in a layered application, apply the rule to catch exceptions at the level that has enough context, implement structured logging with meaningful fields and stack traces, and translate low-level technical exceptions into higher-level domain errors. Each objective maps directly to practice: you will inspect a three-tier flow and choose where to catch and log a database failure; you will set up a structured logger that emits key-value entries and include exception information for operations that fail; you will create a small custom exception like DataStorageError and use it to hide low-level file system details from callers who only need a user-friendly result. These skills matter because they reduce accidental leakage of technical details, make logs searchable and actionable, and keep business logic focused on business concerns. Expect concrete examples and a short hands-on coding activity that exercises these objectives.

Beyond recognizing boundaries, you'll practice concrete logging and translation patterns. You will configure a logger that emits JSON-like entries with timestamp, level, message, module, function name, and exception details. You'll practice raising a custom DataStorageError after catching file system exceptions, and you will test how the presentation layer converts that into a friendly message. We'll also examine log levels and when to use DEBUG versus INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL. Practicing these habits will improve your operational readiness: structured logs make incidents searchable, and exception translation prevents accidental exposure of internals to users. You will finish with a short hands-on test that writes to a file, triggers an error, logs the stack trace, and checks that the caller receives only the custom storage error. This experiment reinforces where to log and what to re-throw.

An error handling boundary is a deliberate place in your architecture where exceptions stop propagating and are either handled, logged, or translated to a different type. This is not an ad-hoc catch anywhere — it is a boundary chosen because that layer has the right context to make a sensible decision. For example, the data access layer knows about S Q L errors and constraints and can translate a unique-constraint violation into a DuplicateEntryError. The business logic layer knows user creation rules and can translate that into UserAlreadyExistsException. The presentation layer knows how to render messages for users and should not be forced to examine S Q L state codes. An important misconception to avoid is thinking every exception must be handled as soon as it appears. Catching too early robs higher layers of context and often leads to leaking technical details into user-facing logic. Another common mistake is catching too broadly; blanket catches hide failures like configuration errors or memory issues. A practical heuristic is: catch where you can do one of three things with confidence — recover, enrich/translate, or fail with context. Example: when a file write fails in a storage module, that module logs the stack trace and raises DataStorageError; callers then show a friendly message. Takeaway: choose boundaries that have the data and intent to act correctly, and avoid catching exceptions without a clear handling strategy. Where in your codebase are you currently catching broad exceptions? Could that be moved to a more contextual boundary?

A three-tier application—Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access—creates natural boundaries for error handling. Errors originate in low-level components like the database, filesystem, or network. The Data Access Layer is responsible for catching technical exceptions such as S Q L errors or IO failures, logging technical details, and then re-throwing a more abstract exception like DatabaseAccessException. The Business Logic Layer receives that higher-level error and, depending on context, may translate it further into a business exception such as UserAlreadyExistsException or PaymentProcessingFailedException. Finally, the Presentation Layer maps business exceptions to user-friendly messages and HTTP responses. A concrete example: a unique constraint violation in the database becomes DuplicateEntryError in the DAL, then UserAlreadyExistsException in the BLL, and finally a 409 conflict with a friendly message in the UI. A common mistake is to let the presentation layer catch raw S Q L exceptions and generate messages using low-level details; that exposes internals and confuses users. Another subtle point: logging must occur at boundaries where the log entry can include meaningful contextual fields. If you log only in low-level code without business context, operational teams may struggle to understand the impact. Where in your stack can you attach identifiers like request ID, user ID, or operation name so logs are actionable?

The phrase "catch at the appropriate level" means you should only catch exceptions in the layer that has enough information to do something useful: fix it, add context, or create a meaningful domain-level error. The practical effect is that each layer stays focused. For example, a DAL knows S Q L error codes and can recognize a unique constraint violation and transform it into a DuplicateEntryError. The BLL knows business rules and can convert that into UserAlreadyExistsException or use a compensating action. If you catch an error too early, say in a helper function deep inside the DAL, you remove knowledge that upstream logic might need to decide how to continue. Conversely, catching too broadly at high levels with a generic exception handler often hides programming errors and control flow bugs. A common misconception is believing that more catches equals more robustness — in fact, poorly placed catches reduce observability and can convert recoverable errors into silent failures. To decide where to catch, ask: can this layer produce a meaningful, context-enriched response to the caller? If yes, catch and handle there; if not, let it bubble to a boundary that can.

Structured logging means emitting entries that are machine-readable, usually key-value pairs or JSON objects, rather than free-form text. This makes logs searchable, filterable, and easier to parse by aggregation tools. Essential fields to include are timestamp, level, message, logger name, module, function, line number, and contextual extras such as request ID, user ID, and operation name. When an exception occurs, include the stack trace so engineers can reconstruct the failure. A misconception is treating logs as informal notes — instead, treat them as structured telemetry that your monitoring and incident tooling will consume. For example, logging an error from a failed data save should include the filename, user identifier, and the original exception detail in an "exception" field. Structured logs also support different levels: DEBUG for verbose diagnostics, INFO for normal operation confirmations, WARNING for notable but non-fatal events, ERROR for failed functions, and CRITICAL for program-halting failures. Takeaway: pick a consistent schema, attach context at boundaries, and avoid mixing unstructured messages with important diagnosis fields.
